subject: DI02000021

intro_text.en: Unit 3 of Engineering Mathematics: integration as the reverse of differentiation, the standard integrals and working rules, substitution, integration by parts, the definite integral with its properties, and the two applications - the area under a curve and the volume of revolution. Twenty-five fully solved numericals, each linked to a card.

h.en: 1.1 The indefinite integral and the constant c

body.en:
Definition

Integration is the reverse of differentiation. If dF/dx = f(x), then ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + c, where c is any constant.

The symbol ∫ means 'integrate', f(x) is the integrand, dx names the variable and the answer F(x) is called the primitive or anti-derivative.

Why the + c is compulsory

x², x² + 3 and x² − 7 all differentiate to 2x, so from the slope alone you cannot recover the height. Every indefinite integral carries + c until a condition (a point on the curve) fixes it.

Worked example

∫ 2x dx = x² + c. If you are also told that the curve passes through (1, 5), then 5 = 1 + c gives c = 4 and the answer is y = x² + 4.

Check every answer

Differentiate the result; it must return the integrand exactly. This one habit catches nearly every integration error.

Rule

∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, valid for every n except n = −1.

Worked examples

∫ x⁵ dx = x⁶/6 + c; ∫ x² dx = x³/3 + c; ∫ x dx = x²/2 + c.

For a root, write it as a power first: ∫ √x dx = ∫ x^(1/2) dx = (2/3)x^(3/2) + c.

For a reciprocal power: ∫ x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c.

The special case n = −1

The rule fails for ∫ x⁻¹ dx because dividing by zero is impossible; the answer is the logarithm: ∫ (1/x) dx = log|x| + c.

Common mistake

Subtracting one instead of adding one. Integration raises the power, differentiation lowers it.

h.en: 1.3 Integrals of sums and constant multiples

body.en:
Rules

  • ∫ [f(x) ± g(x)] dx = ∫ f(x) dx ± ∫ g(x) dx
  • ∫ k f(x) dx = k ∫ f(x) dx for a constant k

Worked example

∫ (3x² + 2x + 1) dx = x³ + x² + x + c - integrate term by term and add one c at the end, never one per term.

Constants

∫ 5 dx = 5x + c, because the derivative of 5x is 5. A bare constant integrates to that constant times x.

Common mistake

Writing a separate + c for every bracket. One constant of integration is enough; three constants would simply combine into one.

What is being asked

The question saysThe answer is
∫ f(x) dxa function plus c
∫ from a to ba number
find the areaa number with square units
find y given dy/dx and a pointa particular curve - find c

Notation

The dx is part of the symbol and tells you the variable: ∫ t² dt is a different question from ∫ t² dx (the latter treats t as a constant, giving t²x + c).

A sanity check on size

Integrating raises the degree by one: a quadratic integrand gives a cubic answer. If your answer has the same degree as the integrand, something went wrong.

Learn these by heart

∫ f(x) dxAnswer
xⁿ (n ≠ −1)xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c
1/xlog|x| + c
eˣeˣ + c
aˣaˣ/log a + c
sin x−cos x + c
cos xsin x + c
sec²xtan x + c
k (constant)kx + c

Reading the table backwards

Each line is a derivative read right to left. Because d(cos x)/dx = −sin x, the integral of sin x carries a minus sign.

Common mistake

Integrating cos x to −sin x. Differentiation of sin x gives +cos x, so the integral of cos x is +sin x.

Three families

  • ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + c - the only function that is its own integral.
  • ∫ (1/x) dx = log|x| + c - the modulus because 1/x exists on both sides of 0.
  • ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/log a + c.

Worked example

∫ (eˣ + 1/x) dx = eˣ + log|x| + c. Differentiating gives eˣ + 1/x straight back.

With a linear inside

∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c: divide by the inside derivative. The same idea gives ∫ e^(−2x) dx = −e^(−2x)/2 + c.

Common mistake

Dropping the modulus in log|x|. For an integrand such as 1/x, negative x is allowed, so the absolute value must stay.

Direct forms

∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c and ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c. A sum integrates term by term: ∫ (sin x − cos x) dx = −cos x − sin x + c.

Squared and product forms

∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c comes straight from d(tan x)/dx = sec²x.

Angles with a coefficient

∫ sin 3x dx = −cos(3x)/3 + c and ∫ cos 5x dx = sin(5x)/5 + c: integrate as usual, then divide by the inside derivative.

Common mistake

Forgetting the division when the angle has a coefficient. Differentiating −cos(3x)/3 gives sin 3x, which proves the factor 3 belongs underneath.

h.en: 2.4 Choosing a method before you start

body.en:
The decision tree

  1. Is it a standard form or a sum of them? Integrate directly.
  2. Does one part look like the derivative of another? Substitute.
  3. Is it a product of unlike functions (x times eˣ, x times sin x, log x alone)? Use parts.

Examples of the choice

IntegrandMethod
3x² + 2xstandard, term by term
2x(x² + 1)³substitution u = x² + 1
x eˣparts with u = x
log xparts with u = log x, dv = dx

Verification

Whatever method you use, differentiate the answer and compare with the integrand. It takes ten seconds and catches the majority of slips.

Idea

If the integrand contains a function and (nearly) its derivative, replace the inner function by u. Then du = u′ dx, and the integral becomes a standard one in u.

Worked example

∫ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx: take u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx. The integral is ∫ u³ du = u⁴/4 + c = (x² + 1)⁴/4 + c.

Check

Differentiating (x² + 1)⁴/4 gives 4(x² + 1)³/4 × 2x = 2x(x² + 1)³, which is the integrand, so the answer is right.

Common mistake

Substituting but forgetting to replace dx. Every dx must be rewritten in terms of du before you integrate.

Good choices

  • Inside a power or root: u = the whole bracket.
  • Inside a logarithm: u = the argument of the log.
  • The denominator: u = the bottom of a fraction.
  • The exponent: u = the power of e.

Examples

∫ (2x + 3)⁴ dx with u = 2x + 3 gives ∫ u⁴ (du/2) = u⁵/10 + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c.

∫ sin³x cos x dx with u = sin x gives ∫ u³ du = sin⁴x/4 + c.

Rule of thumb

After substituting, everything must be in u - if an x survives, the choice was wrong or a constant has to be adjusted.

The constant factor trick

If du is a multiple of what is present, adjust the constant rather than the variable.

Worked example

∫ x(x² + 1)³ dx: u = x² + 1 gives du = 2x dx, but only x dx is present. Write x dx = du/2, so the integral is (1/2)∫ u³ du = (1/2)(u⁴/4) + c = (x² + 1)⁴/8 + c.

Logarithmic results

When the top is exactly the derivative of the bottom, the answer is a logarithm: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx = log(x² + 1) + c.

Common mistake

A constant may be moved in or out; a variable may not. Never write x = du/2 unless the x really cancels.

Two safe routes

  1. Change the limits: when u = x² + 1, the limit x = 0 becomes u = 1 and x = 1 becomes u = 2.
  2. Or integrate in u, put x back, and only then substitute the original limits.

Worked idea

∫₀¹ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx. With u = x² + 1 the limits 0 and 1 become 1 and 2, so the integral is ∫₁² u³ du = [u⁴/4]₁² = 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.

Why limits must follow u

A limit written as 0 refers to x = 0. Once the variable is u, the old limits are meaningless - the most common error in definite substitution.

No + c appears in a definite integral, because it cancels when the limits are subtracted.

Rule

∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du - it comes from the product rule rearranged, and it trades one integral for a simpler one.

Worked example

∫ x eˣ dx: choose u = x (so du = dx) and dv = eˣ dx (so v = eˣ). Then the integral is x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + c = eˣ(x − 1) + c.

Check

Differentiating eˣ(x − 1) gives eˣ(x − 1) + eˣ = x eˣ, the integrand.

Common mistake

Swapping u and dv. Choosing u = eˣ makes the new integral harder, not easier - the point of parts is to reduce the work.

Priority for u

Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic (x, x²), Trig, Exponential - take u as the function that comes first in this list, and dv as the rest.

Why

Logarithms and inverse trig functions have no elementary derivative in the table but become simple when differentiated; exponentials and sines stay simple when integrated.

Examples of the choice

Integraludv
∫ x eˣ dxxeˣ dx
∫ x cos x dxxcos x dx
∫ x log x dxlog xx dx
∫ log x dxlog xdx

Common mistake

Choosing u = x when a logarithm is present. With log in the integrand, u = log x always wins.

h.en: 4.3 Worked examples with trigonometric and logarithmic partners

body.en:
Trigonometric

∫ x cos x dx: u = x, dv = cos x dx, so v = sin x. The integral is x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + c.

Logarithmic with algebra

∫ x log x dx: u = log x, dv = x dx, so du = dx/x and v = x²/2. Then the integral is (x²/2)log x − ∫ (x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2)log x − x²/4 + c.

When parts is needed twice

∫ x² eˣ dx needs two rounds; each round lowers the power of x by one until only eˣ is left.

Common mistake

Leaving the answer as (x²/2)log x − ∫ x/2 dx. The second integral must be evaluated before the answer is complete.

h.en: 4.4 The special case ∫ log x dx

body.en:
A product in disguise

There is only one function, but you may take dv = dx, that is v = x.

Working

u = log x (du = dx/x) and dv = dx (v = x), so ∫ log x dx = x log x − ∫ x(1/x) dx = x log x − ∫ 1 dx = x log x − x + c.

Check

d/dx[x log x − x] = log x + x(1/x) − 1 = log x, so the answer is correct.

Same idea elsewhere

∫ log x dx, ∫ sin⁻¹x dx and ∫ tan⁻¹x dx are all done by taking dv = dx. This is a standard exam pattern worth memorising.

Definition

A definite integral has limits: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), written with square brackets [F(x)] from a to b.

The answer is a number, not a function, and it equals the signed area between the curve and the x-axis from a to b.

Worked example

∫₀² (x² + 1) dx = [x³/3 + x]₀² = (8/3 + 2) − 0 = 14/3.

Why no + c

(F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a): the constant cancels, so it is never written in a definite integral.

Common mistake

Subtracting in the wrong order. The upper limit goes in first: F(b) − F(a), not F(a) − F(b).

Procedure

  1. Find the indefinite integral (ignore c).
  2. Write it in square brackets with the limits.
  3. Substitute the upper limit, then the lower limit, and subtract.
  4. Simplify to a single number.

Worked examples

∫₁³ 2x dx = [x²]₁³ = 9 − 1 = 8.

∫₀^(π/2) sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^(π/2) = 0 − (−1) = 1.

∫₀¹ e^(2x) dx = [e^(2x)/2]₀¹ = (e² − 1)/2.

Check the sign

An area found below the x-axis comes out negative. That is mathematically correct for the integral, but an area question expects the positive value, so split the interval at the crossing point.

The four properties

  • ∫ from a to a = 0
  • ∫ from a to b = − ∫ from b to a (swapping the limits changes the sign)
  • ∫ from a to b = ∫ from a to c + ∫ from c to b (splitting the interval)
  • ∫ from −a to a of an odd function = 0, and of an even function = 2∫ from 0 to a

Using odd and even

x³ is odd, so ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0 without any calculation. x² is even, so ∫₋₂² x² dx = 2∫₀² x² dx = 16/3.

Using the split

If ∫₀¹ f = 2 and ∫₁³ f = 5, then ∫₀³ f = 7. This is how a table of measured values is combined in engineering data work.

Common mistake

Using the odd-function rule on an even function, or forgetting that the rule needs symmetric limits about zero.

Signed area

Above the axis the integral is positive; below it is negative. The total area is the sum of the absolute values, which is why a curve that crosses the axis has to be split.

Example

For y = x from −2 to 2, ∫ x dx = 0, yet the area between the curve and the axis is 2 + 2 = 4: the two triangles cancel in the integral but not in the area.

Engineering reading

An integral of a rate gives a total: ∫ velocity dt is distance, ∫ current dt is charge, ∫ force dx is work. The units of the answer are the units of the integrand times the units of the variable.

Can a definite integral be negative?

Yes - whenever the curve lies below the axis. A negative answer is a warning to stop and think about geometry, not an error in the method.

Rule

The area between y = f(x), the x-axis and the lines x = a and x = b is ∫ from a to b of y dx, provided the curve stays above the axis.

Worked example

Area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3 is ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 9 square units.

Method

  1. Sketch the curve and mark the limits - the sketch tells you whether the area is above or below the axis.
  2. Integrate y with respect to x.
  3. Substitute the limits and subtract.
  4. Take the modulus if the question asks for area and the answer is negative.

Common mistake

Integrating the wrong way round (dx when the boundary is y = c). Read the diagram before choosing the variable.

Why you must split

If the curve crosses the axis between the limits, the integral subtracts the part below. For the area, integrate each piece separately and add the sizes.

Worked example

Area between y = 4x − x² and the x-axis: the curve meets the axis at x = 0 and x = 4 and stays above it in between, so the area is ∫₀⁴ (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3]₀⁴ = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3 square units.

If it crossed

For y = x² − 1 between −2 and 2 the integral is 16/3 − 4 = 4/3, but the true area is 4 (split at x = ±1); the middle piece is below the axis and cancels part of the rest.

Reading the answer

Area is always positive and carries square units (cm², m²). A negative number means the geometry was not checked first.

h.en: 6.3 Area between two curves, and a check

body.en:
Between two curves

When y = f(x) is above y = g(x) on the interval, the area between them is ∫ (f − g) dx. Take the upper curve minus the lower one; the difference is positive.

Example

Between y = x and y = x² from 0 to 1: ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

A quick sanity check

Estimate the area as a rectangle first: width (b − a) times an average height. If the exact answer is far from the estimate, one of the limits or a sign is wrong.

Common mistake

Subtracting the lower curve from the upper one only where they actually cross. Find the crossing points first and use them as limits.

title.en: 7. Volume of Revolution and Exam Routine

h.en: 7.1 Rotating an area about the x-axis

body.en:
Rule

When the area under y = f(x) from a to b is rotated about the x-axis, each thin slice is a disc of radius y and thickness dx, so V = π ∫ y² dx between the limits.

Worked example

y = x from x = 0 to x = 2 rotating about the x-axis: V = π∫₀² x² dx = π[x³/3]₀² = 8π/3 cubic units.

Second example

y = √x from 0 to 4: V = π∫₀⁴ x dx = π[x²/2]₀⁴ = 8π.

Method

  1. Square the given y (or the given x if the rotation is about the y-axis).
  2. Integrate between the limits.
  3. Multiply by π and state the cubic units.

Common mistake

Squaring after integrating. The square is taken first: V = π∫ y² dx, never π(∫ y dx)².

h.en: 7.2 A two-part volume and the shape of the answer

body.en:
One question, two solids

A single question often asks for both y = x (0 to 2) and y = √x (0 to 4). Keep the two results separate and label them; comparing them shows how the shape changes the volume.

Values

y = x gives 8π/3 ≈ 8.38 and y = √x gives 8π ≈ 25.13. The square-root curve encloses far more, because it is further from the axis across most of the interval.

Reading the units

If x and y are in cm, the volume is in cm³. The π is often left in the answer; a decimal is only needed when the question says so.

Common mistake

Using y instead of y². The disc area is πr² with r = y, so the square is unavoidable.

h.en: 7.3 Exam routine for an integration question

body.en:
Five lines that earn the method marks

  1. Write the integral and say which rule or substitution you are using.
  2. Show the substitution or the u and dv, not just the answer.
  3. Integrate and keep the + c (indefinite) or the square brackets (definite).
  4. Substitute the limits carefully, upper first.
  5. For an application, state the units and answer the question that was asked (area, volume, distance).

Time savers

Quote the standard table rather than re-deriving it. Check with differentiation - it takes seconds and settles the answer.

Accuracy habits

Keep fractions rather than converting early to decimals, and put brackets around negative limits. In a definite integral, (−2)² = 4, not −4.

What the examiners reward

A clear statement of the formula, one correct integration and the correct limit arithmetic score nearly all the marks, even if the final simplification is clumsy.

Use the power rule: raise the power by one and divide by the new power.

∫ 6x⁵ dx = 6x⁶/6 + c = x⁶ + c.

Check by differentiating: d(x⁶)/dx = 6x⁵, which is exactly the integrand, so the answer is right.

Integrate term by term: 4x³ gives x⁴, −6x gives −3x², and 5 gives 5x.

So the answer is x⁴ − 3x² + 5x + c.

Check: differentiating x⁴ − 3x² + 5x gives 4x³ − 6x + 5, exactly the integrand, so no term has been lost.

Both terms are standard forms: 3/x integrates to 3 log|x| and eˣ to eˣ.

So the answer is 3 log|x| + eˣ + c.

The modulus is needed because 3/x exists for negative x as well.

Integrate cos to sin and divide by the derivative of the angle, which is 4.

∫ cos 4x dx = sin(4x)/4 + c.

Check: differentiating sin(4x)/4 gives 4 cos(4x)/4 = cos 4x, so the division by the angle's derivative is correct.

Substitute u = 3x + 2, so du = 3 dx and dx = du/3.

The integral becomes (1/3)∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/18 + c = (3x + 2)⁶/18 + c.

Check: differentiating (3x + 2)⁶/18 gives 6(3x + 2)⁵ × 3/18 = (3x + 2)⁵, so the answer is correct.

Take u = x³ + 1, so du = 3x² dx, that is x² dx = du/3.

The integral becomes (1/3)∫ u⁴ du = u⁵/15 + c = (x³ + 1)⁵/15 + c.

Check by differentiating: 5(x³ + 1)⁴ × 3x²/15 = x²(x³ + 1)⁴.

The numerator is the derivative of the denominator: d(x² + x)/dx = 2x + 1.

So with u = x² + x the integral is ∫ du/u = log|u| + c = log|x² + x| + c.

The modulus matters here, because x² + x is negative for x between −1 and 0.

h.en: Practice 8. Evaluate ∫ x sin x dx by parts.

body.en:
Take u = x (du = dx) and dv = sin x dx (v = −cos x).

∫ x sin x dx = −x cos x − ∫ (−cos x) dx = −x cos x + sin x + c.

Check: differentiating gives −cos x + x sin x + cos x = x sin x.

h.en: Practice 9. Evaluate ∫ x² log x dx.

body.en:
By LIATE choose u = log x and dv = x² dx, so du = dx/x and v = x³/3.

The integral = (x³/3)log x − ∫ (x³/3)(1/x) dx = (x³/3)log x − ∫ (x²/3) dx.

So the answer is (x³/3)log x − x³/9 + c.

Integrate: [x² + 3x]₁².

Upper limit: 4 + 6 = 10. Lower limit: 1 + 3 = 4.

The value is 10 − 4 = 6, and no + c is written because the constant cancels in a definite integral.

Substitute u = x², so du = 2x dx and x dx = du/2. The limits 0 and 1 become 0 and 1.

The integral is (1/2)∫₀¹ eᵘ du = (1/2)[eᵘ]₀¹ = (e − 1)/2.

Numerically this is about 0.859.

The integral of cos x is sin x, so the value is [sin x] from 0 to π/2.

sin(π/2) = 1 and sin 0 = 0, so the answer is 1.

The area under one quarter of the cosine curve is exactly 1 square unit.

h.en: Practice 13. Find the area under y = x³ from x = 0 to x = 2.

body.en:
The curve is above the axis on 0 to 2, so the area is ∫₀² x³ dx.

= [x⁴/4]₀² = 16/4 = 4.

The area is 4 square units; a rectangle of the same width with average height 2 would have the same area.

h.en: Practice 14. Find the area between y = x² and the x-axis from x = 1 to x = 3.

body.en:
The curve is above the axis throughout, so the area is ∫₁³ x² dx.

= [x³/3]₁³ = 27/3 − 1/3 = 26/3.

The area is 26/3 ≈ 8.67 square units. The average height over the interval is the area divided by the width, about 4.33, which sits between the curve heights 1 and 9.

h.en: Practice 15. Find the volume when y = √x is rotated about the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 4.

body.en:
Each slice is a disc of radius y = √x, so V = π∫₀⁴ y² dx = π∫₀⁴ x dx.

= π[x²/2]₀⁴ = π(8 − 0) = 8π.

The volume is 8π ≈ 25.13 cubic units, and the answer is left in terms of π because the question gives no decimals.

Use the power rule: raise the power by one and divide by the new power.

∫ x⁵ dx = x⁶/6 + c.

Check: d(x⁶/6)/dx = 6x⁵/6 = x⁵, which is the integrand.

Integrate term by term: 3x² gives x³, 2x gives x², and 1 gives x.

So the answer is x³ + x² + x + c.

Check: 3x² + 2x + 1, exactly the integrand.

Write the root as a power: √x = x^(1/2).

∫ x^(1/2) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + c = (2/3)x^(3/2) + c.

In root form this is (2/3)x√x + c.

Write the integrand as a power: 1/x² = x⁻².

∫ x⁻² dx = x⁻¹/(−1) + c = −1/x + c.

Check: d(−x⁻¹)/dx = x⁻² = 1/x².

Both parts are standard forms: eˣ integrates to eˣ and 1/x integrates to log|x|.

So the answer is eˣ + log|x| + c.

The modulus sign is needed because 1/x is defined for negative x as well.

∫ sin x dx = −cos x and ∫ cos x dx = sin x, so the difference is −cos x − sin x + c.

Check: differentiating gives sin x − cos x, the integrand.

Watch the double negative: −(−sin x) = +sin x.

Let u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx. The limits change too: x = 0 gives u = 1 and x = 1 gives u = 2.

The integral becomes ∫₁² u³ du = [u⁴/4]₁² = 4 − 1/4 = 15/4.

No + c appears, and the old limits must not be used with u.

Substitute u = 2x + 3, so du = 2 dx and dx = du/2.

The integral becomes (1/2)∫ u⁴ du = u⁵/10 + c = (2x + 3)⁵/10 + c.

Check: 5(2x + 3)⁴ × 2/10 = (2x + 3)⁴.

Take u = x² + 1, so du = 2x dx, that is x dx = du/2.

The integral becomes (1/2)∫ u³ du = u⁴/8 + c = (x² + 1)⁴/8 + c.

Check by differentiating: 4(x² + 1)³ × 2x/8 = x(x² + 1)³.

The numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so the answer is a logarithm.

With u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx, the integral is ∫ du/u = log|u| + c = log(x² + 1) + c.

No modulus is needed because x² + 1 is always positive.

Take u = sin x, so du = cos x dx.

The integral becomes ∫ u³ du = u⁴/4 + c = sin⁴x/4 + c.

Check: 4 sin³x cos x/4 = sin³x cos x, the integrand.

q.en: Evaluate ∫ x eˣ dx by parts.

a.en:
Take u = x (du = dx) and dv = eˣ dx (v = eˣ).

∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du = x eˣ − ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + c.

So the answer is eˣ(x − 1) + c. Check: eˣ(x − 1) + eˣ = x eˣ.

q.en: Evaluate ∫ x cos x dx by parts.

a.en:
Take u = x (du = dx) and dv = cos x dx (v = sin x).

The integral is x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x − (−cos x) + c = x sin x + cos x + c.

Check: differentiating gives sin x + x cos x − sin x = x cos x.

By LIATE the logarithm becomes u: u = log x (du = dx/x) and dv = x dx (v = x²/2).

The integral = (x²/2)log x − ∫ (x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2)log x − ∫ (x/2) dx.

So the answer is (x²/2)log x − x²/4 + c.

There is one function, so take u = log x and dv = dx, giving v = x.

∫ log x dx = x log x − ∫ x(1/x) dx = x log x − ∫ 1 dx = x log x − x + c.

Check: log x + 1 − 1 = log x.

Integrate: [x³/3 + x]₀².

Upper limit: 8/3 + 2 = 14/3. Lower limit: 0.

So the value is 14/3. No + c is written in a definite integral.

The integral of 2x is x², so the definite integral is [x²]₁³.

9 − 1 = 8.

Check by geometry: the area is a trapezium with parallel sides 2 and 6 and width 2, that is (2 + 6)/2 × 2 = 8.

The integral of sin x is −cos x, so the value is [−cos x] from 0 to π/2.

cos(π/2) = 0 and cos 0 = 1, so 0 − (−1) = 1.

The area under one arch of the sine curve from 0 to π/2 is exactly 1 square unit.

The integral of e^(2x) is e^(2x)/2 (divide by the inside derivative).

So the value is [e^(2x)/2]₀¹ = (e² − 1)/2.

Numerically (7.389 − 1)/2 ≈ 3.19, which is reasonable for a curve rising from 1 to 7.4.

q.en: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx using a property.

a.en:
x³ is an odd function: f(−x) = −f(x).

For an odd function the integral over symmetric limits is zero, so ∫₋₁¹ x³ dx = 0.

Check directly: [x⁴/4]₋₁¹ = 1/4 − 1/4 = 0. The areas above and below the axis cancel.

q.en: If ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = 2 and ∫₁³ f(x) dx = 5, find ∫₀³ f(x) dx.

a.en:
Use the splitting property: the integral over 0 to 3 is the sum of the two pieces.

∫₀³ f = ∫₀¹ f + ∫₁³ f = 2 + 5 = 7.

This is how a table of measured values is combined when the readings stop at a point.

q.en: Find the area under y = x² from x = 0 to x = 3.

a.en:
The curve is above the axis on this interval, so the area is ∫₀³ x² dx.

= [x³/3]₀³ = 27/3 − 0 = 9.

The area is 9 square units. Integrating raises the degree, so the answer divided by the width (3) gives an average height of 3, which matches the curve at its midpoint.

q.en: Find the area between y = 4x − x² and the x-axis.

a.en:
First find where the curve meets the axis: 4x − x² = x(4 − x) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 4.

The curve is above the axis between them, so the area is ∫₀⁴ (4x − x²) dx = [2x² − x³/3]₀⁴.

= 32 − 64/3 = 96/3 − 64/3 = 32/3 ≈ 10.67 square units.

q.en: Find the volume when y = x is rotated about the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2.

a.en:
Each slice is a disc of radius y = x, so V = π∫ y² dx.

V = π∫₀² x² dx = π[x³/3]₀² = 8π/3.

The volume is 8π/3 ≈ 8.38 cubic units - a cone of height 2 and base radius 2, which has volume (1/3)πr²h = 8π/3 exactly.

q.en: Find the volume when y = √x is rotated about the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 4.

a.en:
The radius of each slice is y = √x, so V = π∫ y² dx = π∫₀⁴ x dx.

= π[x²/2]₀⁴ = π(8 − 0) = 8π.

The volume is 8π ≈ 25.13 cubic units, three times the volume of the cone in the previous example because the curve stays further from the axis.
The reverse of differentiation: finding a function whose derivative is the given integrand.

q.en: Why does an indefinite integral end with + c?

a.en: Because every constant differentiates to zero, so all the curves F(x) + c have the same slope. A condition on the curve fixes c.

q.en: What is the difference between a definite and an indefinite integral?

a.en: An indefinite integral gives a function plus c; a definite integral has limits and gives a number.

q.en: Why is there no + c in a definite integral?

a.en: The constant cancels when the limits are subtracted: (F(b) + c) − (F(a) + c) = F(b) − F(a).

q.en: What is ∫ (1/x) dx and why is the modulus there?

a.en: log|x| + c. The modulus is needed because 1/x is defined for negative x too, and log of a negative number does not exist.
When one part of the integrand is (a constant multiple of) the derivative of another part, so the integral reduces to a standard form in u.

q.en: In a definite integral, what must be done to the limits after substituting?

a.en: They must be converted to the new variable using u = g(x); keeping the old x-limits with a u-integral is a common error.

q.en: State the formula for integration by parts.

a.en: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.

q.en: How do you choose u in integration by parts?

a.en: By LIATE: logarithm, inverse trig, algebraic, trigonometric, exponential - u is the function that comes first in the list.

q.en: How do you integrate log x?

a.en: By parts with u = log x and dv = dx, giving x log x − x + c.

q.en: How can you check any indefinite integral?

a.en: Differentiate the answer; it must give the integrand back exactly.

q.en: What does a definite integral represent geometrically?

a.en: The signed area between the curve and the x-axis over the interval: positive above the axis, negative below it.

q.en: How do you find the area under a curve?

a.en: Integrate y with respect to x between the two limits, splitting the interval where the curve crosses the axis.

q.en: Give the formula for the volume of revolution about the x-axis.

a.en: V = π ∫ y² dx between the limits, because each slice is a disc of radius y.

q.en: Why is y squared in the volume formula?

a.en: The disc area is πr² with r = y, so the square comes from the geometry of the circle, not from the integration.

q.en: What happens to the sign of an integral when the limits are swapped?

a.en: The sign changes: ∫ from a to b = − ∫ from b to a.

q.en: An integral of zero over symmetric limits - what does it mean?

a.en: The areas above and below the axis are equal in size; this always happens for an odd function such as x³.
